articles.title: 9/11 has had a lasting effect on world affairs
articles.summary: Reflecting on twenty-five years since the Sept. 11 attacks, Stuart Gottlieb examines how the tragedy reshaped American foreign policy, shifted focus toward non-state actors, redefined terrorism as warfare, and emphasized the need for a long-term battle of ideas.
articles.body:
On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, I was driving to Capitol Hill, where I worked as a Senate foreign policy adviser. I heard on the radio that a small plane had crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center. Terrible accident, I assumed.

As I approached my garage entrance, another report said that a second plane had hit the South Tower, and that they had both been commercial airliners. This was no accident. As I sat silently in my car before entering the chaos of that day, I thought to myself, nothing will ever be the same again.

Twenty-five years later, life has gone on, new challenges have arisen, and the U.S. has been spared a second 9/11. Yet the profound impact of that day still resounds. An attack worse than Pearl Harbor had been carried out with pinpoint precision by the shadowy al Qaeda terror organization. Ever since, the prevention of terrorism has dominated American foreign policy much as containing communism did during the Cold War. And as with the Cold War, there have been ups and downs, successes and failures, and multiple reassessments along the way.

But the most significant effect of 9/11 was how it instantly shattered the conventional wisdom at the time regarding global threats, combating terrorism, and America’s role in the world generally. Four major rethinks from that period last to this day and continue as pragmatic guideposts for ensuring terrorism remains a manageable problem for another 25 years.

First was the end of what Francis Fukuyama had called “ the end of history .” Perhaps the greatest shock of 9/11 was that it occurred at all. At the time, the U.S. was still basking in its post-Cold War “unipolar moment.” All the talk in American and Western circles was about promoting universal liberal values and neoliberal economics.

But looking back, plenty of history was still swirling in the 1990s in the form of vicious civil wars, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and escalating terrorist attacks against the U.S., culminating in 9/11. That the first major post-Soviet threat to American security came from a terrorist group showed both the significance of terrorism in contemporary world politics and the cost of neglecting non-Western and less-developed parts of the world. The decades since have grown even more complex with the emergence of state-based challenges to the Western-led international order from China, Russia, Iran and others.

Second was the rise of the transnational terrorist organization as a world actor. For centuries, states have been the primary actors in world politics, as seen with the United Nations being composed of “member states.” On 9/11, this state-centric system was rattled to its core. What makes al-Qaeda and related militant Islamist movements such as Islamic State uniquely difficult and dangerous is that they function as powerful non-state global actors. For example, al-Qaeda lost its base in Afghanistan in 2001, and the Islamic State group lost its “caliphate” in 2019, yet both have been actively operating through franchises across Africa, the Middle East, South Asia, and elsewhere, patiently planning for future attacks against states.

Having no government to negotiate with, threaten or cajole has fundamentally altered the nature of national security strategy in the 21st century. It is why, 25 years after 9/11, and despite two failed wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, America remains extremely forwardly deployed in its efforts to thwart terrorism. As of 2023, U.S. forces were conducting counterterrorism operations in at least 78 countries .

Third is the shift toward treating terrorism as a form of warfare. Prior to 9/11, the U.S. treated terrorism primarily as a criminal justice matter. That makes sense considering our robust legal system and the fact that terrorism involves the commission of crimes. It also made sense because most terrorism of that era (for example, the Palestine Liberation Organization and Irish Republican Army) revolved around small-scale attacks to gain attention for a cause — what terrorism expert Brian Jenkins summarized as “a lot of people watching, not a lot of people dead.”

On 9/11, a new terrorism exploded onto the world scene, far more interested in mass destruction than messaging. Instead of limited political goals, al Qaeda and its cohort were seeking a sustained global war against America, the West and their supporters. Both Republicans and Democrats recognize that this requires measures well beyond civilian courtrooms. For example, Barack Obama promised “to reverse” George W. Bush’s use of aggressive wartime powers but then expanded Bush’s controversial drone assassinations program overseas and surveillance program at home. He also placed such policies under greater Constitutional scrutiny, permitting a more legitimate long-term effort.

Finally 9/11 shattered the notion that Islamist terrorism was a fringe threat — it spawns from a centuries-old militant ideology that enjoys considerable support around the world . This helps explain how al Qaeda and ISIS survive losses of their top leaders, and why the movement cannot simply be defeated on a military battlefield — it must be confronted in a battle of ideas.

A strategy to “defeat an ideology, not just a group of people” was a key recommendation of the bipartisan 9/11 Commission Report; it remains equally important today. Over the last 25 years, Washington has leaned heavily on military and surveillance tools to combat Islamist militancy, while giving short shrift to winning hearts and minds in regions vulnerable to extremism. To succeed over the long run, the U.S. must soften its use of military power and prove itself a vital partner in economic expansion and improving the lives of communities in Muslim countries and the developing world generally.

Since 9/11, American efforts have weakened global terrorism and prevented worst-case-scenario attacks. But militant Islamist groups are notoriously patient. A quarter-century may have passed, but the U.S. must maintain its post-9/11 vigilance while better addressing the stubborn support that exists for these movements worldwide.

Stuart Gottlieb teaches American foreign policy and counterterrorism at Columbia University, where he is a member of the Saltzman Institute of War & Peace Studies. He served as a foreign policy adviser and speechwriter in the United States Senate from 1999 to 2003.

articles.title: El-Sayed on GOP convention attendee’s call for him to be shot: ‘Call it out for what it is’
articles.summary: Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Thursday that he hoped Republicans would “call it out for what it is” when discussing shouts from a GOP midterm convention attendee who called for him and other Democratic lawmakers to be shot. In an interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, El-Sayed was asked about a clip that showed a member…
articles.body:
Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Thursday that he hoped Republicans would “call it out for what it is” when discussing shouts from a GOP midterm convention attendee who called for him and other Democratic lawmakers to be shot.

In an interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, El-Sayed was asked about a clip that showed a member of the audience shouting, “He should be shot,” while Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) listed Democrats during his Thursday remarks, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico.

It is unclear if Cruz could hear the audience member from the stage as he did not acknowledge the shouts. The incident came on the first anniversary of conservative political commentator Charlie Kirk’s assassination, an occasion marked at the GOP convention, including by Cruz during his speech Thursday.

“Look, I’m a dad with two daughters, and I hope those daughters get to grow up and live with their dad. This is what has become norm in our politics, I mean, literally calls to violence and the inability for anybody to actually call it out,” El-Sayed told Collins.

“We can learn to disagree agreeably, and when you hear that kind of call to violence, it should be shuddering to all of us. We have a responsibility to lower the temperature, to realize that this is not a blood sport, where you’re just trying to bash the other guy,” he said.

“And so I hope that everybody who heard that is going to call it out for what it is: a call to violence that ought to be condemned across the board,” he continued.

El-Sayed concluded that he hoped “we can actually turn our politics back into a conversation about what really matters,” which he said comprised “the ability to live a dignified life, get the things that you need and deserve in your life.”

He led his opponent , former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), by 3 points in a Wednesday CNN poll, with 47 percent support to the GOP candidate’s 44 percent.

The race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) has been hotly contested, as both parties hope to take the Senate majority.

Cruz’s office did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

articles.title: Joe diGenova resigns from DOJ position investigating Trump foes
articles.summary: Joe diGenova, a Trump ally tapped to lead a sprawling investigation into many of the president’s perceived enemies, resigned from his post late Thursday, indicating concerns over the strength of the case. The so-called grand conspiracy investigation was led out of a U.S. attorney office in Florida where prosecutors issued dozens of subpoenas in a…
articles.body:
Joe diGenova, a Trump ally tapped to lead a sprawling investigation into many of the president’s perceived enemies, resigned from his post late Thursday, indicating concerns over the strength of the case.

The so-called grand conspiracy investigation was led out of a U.S. attorney office in Florida where prosecutors issued dozens of subpoenas in a sweeping probe into the 2016 election and the cases into President Trump.

“I did in fact resign,” diGenova told The Associated Press, calling it an “honor and a privilege” to serve Trump and the Department of Justice (DOJ).

But in a later interview with the New York Post, diGenova suggested there were larger issues with the investigation.

“If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem,” he told the outlet.

The Trump ally later expanded on those comments to The Associated Press, saying, “There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”

The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment. ABC News first reported his resignation.

The probe has yet to lead to any charges.

Throughout the course of the investigation, prosecutors have been focused on former CIA Director John Brennan, who in July sued to prompt the preservation of all files related to a potential case.

Prosecutors have also sought information from those who worked on the Mar-a-Lago documents case into Trump.

articles.title: Why Trump is leaning into his role as ‘builder-in-chief’
articles.summary: Donald Trump is shifting focus from the ongoing conflict with Iran toward several major architectural renovation projects across Washington, D.C.
articles.body:
You’d think that a self-described genius like President Trump would have more sense than to post an AI-generated image on social media declaring “ Mission Accomplished ” in Iran.

For one thing, the mission is not accomplished. Iran still has the capacity to build a nuclear bomb, and missiles are still flying over the Strait of Hormuz.

So how exactly is the mission accomplished?

And you’d think the president might have learned something from another president — George W. Bush, who stood in front of a giant “Mission Accomplished” banner aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln when the war in Iraq was not even close to being over.

Mission accomplished became a symbol of failure — and ammunition for the war’s critics.

But there’s something else intriguing about all of this.

With no end in sight to the conflict with Iran, Trump seems eager to change the subject. And what would he rather talk about if not missiles or nuclear enrichment or the Strait of Hormuz?

He’d rather talk about architecture than a war he calls “small potatoes.”

More specifically, he’d rather talk about how he’s changing the face of the White House — and a good part of Washington along with it.

He loves talking about his grand, gold-laced ballroom. Then there’s the magnificent 250-foot triumphal arch, sometimes called the Arch de Trump. And there’s the Reflecting Pool he’s trying to make look — if not exactly beautiful — at least halfway decent.

As for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, he’s still trying to rename it, with his name getting top billing. And there’s the facelift he wants to give a public golf course near the National Mall .

The president doesn’t like the looks of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, so he’s pushing to have the granite exterior of the historic structure painted white . And he’d like to build a garden honoring 250 notable Americans , complete with life-size statues, reflecting pools, plazas and an amphitheater.

As The New York Times put it , “As the United States appears mired in another intractable conflict in the Middle East, Mr. Trump has basked in the momentum he has on the half-dozen makeover projects he has set in motion throughout the capital.”

The Times also reports that “He is at his most animated, aides and visitors to the White House say, when he is showing off the designs for the ballroom, boasting about the size of the columns and their designs.”

“Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, no other president has done more to beautify our nation’s interior than President Trump,” a White House spokesman said.

And maybe “Builder-in-Chief” tells us more than the spokesman intended.

Because building is a lot easier to talk about than Iran.

A ballroom has blueprints. An arch has dimensions. A building can be painted white. And when somebody asks how the project is going, the president can point to something and say: Look what I built.

Wars don’t always follow the plans. The other side gets a vote. Enemies don’t necessarily cooperate with your timetable. And when you declare “Mission Accomplished,” inconvenient things can keep happening — missiles can still fly, ships can still come under attack, and the mission can stubbornly refuse to be accomplished.

Which may explain why Trump seems so much more comfortable talking about columns and ballrooms than about how and when the war with Iran is actually going to end.

“I’m a really good builder,” Trump told reporters earlier this year. “The thing I do best in life is build.”

And given the choice between explaining a war he hasn’t figured out how to end and showing reporters a ballroom he knows exactly how he wants to finish, is there really any mystery about which Trump would rather talk about?

One last thing: When was the last time you heard the president refer to his grand ballroom or the “Arch de Trump” as “small potatoes”?

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page .

articles.title: Former presidents reflect on 9/11: ‘We can’t erase the nightmare’
articles.summary: Former American presidents on Friday reflected on the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks as the U.S. marks the 25th anniversary of the tragic day. “We can’t erase the nightmare that so many have lived through and are still living with today, but we can support the people who have given and lost so much by…
articles.body:
Former American presidents on Friday reflected on the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks as the U.S. marks the 25th anniversary of the tragic day.

“We can’t erase the nightmare that so many have lived through and are still living with today, but we can support the people who have given and lost so much by treating one another with respect, in person and online, and recognizing that what we have in common is far more important than what divides us,” former President Clinton wrote in a statement .

“As 9/11 moves further from lived experience into history, may we always take this solemn anniversary to come together and keep alive the memories of all who were lost,” he continued. “We owe that to them, to their loved ones, to each other, and to future generations.”

All living former heads of state and Vice President Vance are attending a Friday ceremony at Ground Zero in New York City. President Trump is participating in a memorial at the Pentagon, joined by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, first lady Melania Trump and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice.

A total of 2,977 people died during the attacks on the World Trade Center in New York City; the Pentagon in Arlington, Va.; and at the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93 in Pennsylvania.

In a statement released Friday , former President Obama commemorated the lives lost during the attacks and commended the rescue workers who responded that day.

“Today Michelle and I are remembering those we lost that day, and those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the wars that followed,” Obama wrote.

“We pray for their families,” he continued. “And we hope Americans everywhere remember the true lesson of 9/11: that we can survive even our darkest days as long as we move forward as one nation and one people.”

Former President Biden said the nation will “never forget” this tragic day.

“Twenty-five years ago today, we lost 2,977 souls and in the years since, thousands more to illnesses caused by the attack on our country,” Biden wrote in a Friday social media post .

“This morning, Jill and I hold close the families who carry that loss every day,” he continued. “We honor the heroes of September 11th: the firefighters and police officers who rushed into the towers and the Pentagon, the passengers who fought back over Shanksville, and the generation that stepped up to serve in the aftermath. Even now, we remember the greatest lesson of one of our nation’s darkest days: at our most vulnerable, unity is our most powerful strength.”

Former President George W. Bush, who was serving as president during the attacks, reflected on his administration’s response to the attacks during a Wednesday conversation with Rice at his presidential library in Dallas.

Bush recalled the moment his White House chief of staff, Andrew Card, informed him during an event with schoolchildren that the second World Trade Center tower had been struck.

“I didn’t have much time to process that, but it was pretty clear to me that if we were under attack, that my job was to defend the child that was reading to me and her family and her country,” he said. “And so, it was a moment of clarity.”

The former commander in chief added, “I knew we had to gather evidence, and we had to gather the facts, but I assumed we were under attack.”

articles.title: Collins: Trump’s proposed $5K dividend ‘extraordinarily costly’
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said President Trump’s proposal to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win the midterm elections “would be extraordinarily costly” and questioned providing it to everyone regardless of financial need. “From the few details we have, it seems that the proposed $5,000 dividend would not have an income cap and…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said President Trump’s proposal to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win the midterm elections “would be extraordinarily costly” and questioned providing it to everyone regardless of financial need.

“From the few details we have, it seems that the proposed $5,000 dividend would not have an income cap and would be extraordinarily costly,” Collins said in a statement.

“Tax and spending decisions should be made based on the needs of the American people and the state of the economy, they should not appear to be tied to election results,” she said.

Collins has emerged as one of the highest-profile GOP critics of the proposal , which would cost more than $1 trillion and add to the nation’s $40 trillion debt unless Congress finds a way to offset it.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) defended the idea during an interview with Fox News as a proposal to put more money into the pockets of Americans.

But Thune hesitated on whether the GOP-controlled Senate would take up the proposal on the floor and attempt to pass it.

“Well, that’s a good question,” he said. “We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it.”

Fiscal conservatives have panned the idea.

Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.), a past chair of the House Freedom Caucus, dismissed the proposal as a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

articles.title: Live updates: Trump, Vance, past presidents pause to remember Sept. 11
articles.summary: President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are attending a remembrance at the Pentagon, while Vice President Vance has joined past presidents and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) at Ground Zero on Friday morning, as America pauses to honor the victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. While the memorial in New…
articles.body:
President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are attending a remembrance at the Pentagon , while Vice President Vance has joined past presidents and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) at Ground Zero on Friday morning, as America pauses to honor the victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

While the memorial in New York includes no politics, remarks from Trump and Hegseth at the Pentagon memorial both raised the Iran conflict amid remembrances of those lost.

Twenty-five years after four jets took down the World Trade Center, crashed into the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania, the Trump administration is stepping gingerly into a loosening of tight airport security measures implemented in the aftermath.

Mamdani, a Muslim, has faced criticism for plans to attend the ceremony at Ground Zero. Some 9/11 families, along with former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani (R), have cited past critical remarks from Mamdani’s political allies.

The solemn day follows two days of cheerleading in Dallas for the Trump administration and Republican midterm candidates. Vance closed the convention amid growing chatter about his 2028 prospects. His Thursday night keynote offered the vice president a chance to charm the base that will be critical if he decides to run to succeed Trump in the next election.

The president will return to the White House for signing time before departing later Friday for Dublin. He’ll spend the weekend at his golf resort for the Irish Open.

articles.title: US must adopt the Finland model for producing warships
articles.summary: The situation is dire: We need to stop thinking primarily about protecting jobs and start thinking about producing ships at scale.
articles.body:
Last month, President Trump issued a memorandum on “Rebuilding the United States Navy and America’s Shipbuilding Industrial Base.” It called for the Navy to adopt what it terms the “Finland Model” for warship construction.

The memo states that “this Finland Model” is to be used to produce surface ships for anti-submarine warfare, “consolidated cargo replenishment” tankers, and “roll-on, roll-off vessels.”

The arrangement, whose official designation is the Icebreaker Collaboration Agreement or ICEPact , is a three way agreement among the U.S., Canada and Finland to modernize the American and Canadian icebreaker fleets. The deal will enable the Coast Guard to acquire four icebreakers from Finland, with seven more to be built in American shipyards. As a result, the Coast Guard will be able to replace its aging icebreaker fleet quickly.

Construction on the first of the Coast Guard Arctic Security Cutters began in June at the Sata Shipbuilding yard in Finland. Delivery of the icebreaker is on schedule and according to local observers in Helsinki, the program also is on budget.

Two months earlier, the Bollinger shipyard in Houma, La. welded together the first steel sheets of an Arctic Security Cutter design for an icebreaker being built in parallel with a second Finnish shipbuilder, Rauma Marine Constructions.

Trump’s memorandum incorporates several aspects of the Finland model. It requires that foreign shipbuilders building U.S. military craft establish a robust presence within the U.S., building shipyards and hiring U.S. workers even as they build ships abroad. They must also license their “proprietary shipbuilding techniques and technologies” to U.S. shipyards and create U.S. supply chains “for construction and maintenance of all ships” they build in the U.S.

The Finland model offers a blueprint that would enable the US Navy to begin to address its urgent need to increase its force levels and create lasting naval shipbuilding capacity. It holds out the prospects for additional serial warship production, incorporating advanced propulsion and a resilient supplier base.

The Finland model will also yield a capable workforce. Like shipbuilding more generally, Arctic shipbuilding depends on welders, pipefitters, electricians, naval architects, marine engineers, propulsion specialists, and shipyard supervisors. The workforce that emerges from the ICEPact Program would be a welcome addition to the current workforce supporting naval construction.

In order to implement Trump’s plan, foreign shipyards would have to receive some sort of waiver from the State Department’s International Traffic in Arms Regulations which constrain the export of technical data that would be needed to construct the ships to the Navy’s specifications. In addition, ships built in foreign yards would have to allow for both stringent Navy redundancy and survivability standards and for the insertion of the Navy’s combat systems once they are towed to American yards.

It is not impossible to find ways to accommodate whatever technical and other restrictions that might be imposed on foreign shipbuilders. On the other hand, it is far more difficult to win Congressional approval for employing the Finland model for construction of surface combatants.

The administration’s plan has already run into heavy congressional opposition. Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), home to the Bath Iron Works shipyard, has successfully inserted an amendment to the pending fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act that specifies that no fiscal 2027 funds can be obligated for procurement of a battle force ship to be built outside the U.S. His express purpose is to “block [the] Pentagon from sending U.S. shipbuilding jobs overseas.” Not surprisingly, Golden has the support of representatives from other shipbuilding states.

Were the shipyards suffering from bare order books, Golden and those who support his amendment would have a case for restricting overseas shipbuilding for the Navy. But that is not true at all. As the Government Accountability Office’s director of contracting and national security acquisitions testified before two Congressional subcommittees in April, the shipyards are not even meeting construction schedules for ships already under contract. A shortage of backlogs is not the problem.

With China projected to have a battle force of 435 ships by 2030, as compared to the U.S. Navy’s goal of reaching 381 ships more than a decade later, it is imperative that members of Congress, even those who hail from states with shipyards, reconsider their opposition to applying the Finland model to Navy warships.

That model would not only provide the Navy with more ships more quickly, but it would actually accomplish what those members are seeking: more jobs at home for an expanded and well-trained American workforce.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

articles.title: JD Vance is right about stay-at-home parents — but his solution is all wrong
articles.summary: Vance is right that parents should have more opportunities to spend time with their young children. But instead of paying people not to work, why not give businesses stronger incentives to make it easier for working parents to stay home when they need to?
articles.body:
Should the federal government pay parents to stay at home so they can better raise their children?

The Trump administration thinks so, and is working on plans to allow a stay-at-home spouse to collect as much as $9,000 per child each year, depending on their economic circumstances, from funds potentially available from the Health and Human Services Department.

The driver of the program appears to be Vice President Vance, who has long championed more traditional family values where parents and “young children are clearly happier and healthier when they spend the day at home with a parent.”

Vance is right that parents should have more opportunities to spend time with their young children. But instead of paying people not to work, why not give businesses stronger incentives to make it easier for working parents to stay home when they need to?

Sorry if I sound so cynical, but like so many government programs, this one will almost certainly be abused.

Federal programs have had a long history of fraud, stretching from welfare, Medicare, housing and farming subsidy overpayments to the awards of food stamps, school lunches, unemployment and, most recently, COVID payments to people who did not qualify or simply swindled the government. Do we have any doubt that this handout will suffer the same consequences?

And who’s going to enforce this new program? The federal government, whose workforce has shrunk 10 percent since President Trump took office? And who will be eligible? Mothers? Fathers? Aunts? Uncles?

Good luck figuring that out — and then stopping the payments once they have started.

The $12 billion fund that Vance is targeting would mostly be distributed to states, which would then provide the funding for dependent care facilities, providers and assistance. I’m sure that’s not being abused either, right? We’ve already learned, thanks to the investigative work of some independent journalists like Nick Shirley, that most local governments not only have insufficient resources to distribute, monitor and enforce these programs but that some politicians in certain states — hello, Minnesota and California — may have, allegedly, turned a blind eye to funds being distributed to communities that could provide them with votes.

It’s interesting that the Trump administration, a vocal backer of free markets, would put forth a program that is so much the antithesis of capitalism. At a time when many employers complain they can’t find enough workers, should taxpayers be paying some workers to leave the labor force?

If you choose to have kids, you have to make hard choices. Do both Mom and Dad have to work? If they want to afford private schools, summer camps, eating out, Netflix, Disney vacations or car leases, then sure. Good for them. We live in a great country with a high standard of living. But do the taxpayers have to pay for these choices?

Our political leaders need to make choices, too. Who doesn’t like to get paid to stay at home with our kids? But aren’t there other, more pressing priorities for our taxpayer funds? Paying down the deficit? Providing more for the military? Saving Social Security and Medicare? Reducing health care costs? Building better roads? Better schools?

Why not take the funds that the vice president wants to spend on his stay-at-home program and put it toward those pressing needs? As much as we like to think it does, our government does not have a bottomless pit of money. I’m not sure I’d put this at the top of my list of priorities.

What’s more, we already have a number of government-funded tax benefits to encourage child care.

There is a generous individual and family tax credit , which was just expanded in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Employers get credits for providing or referring employees to day care facilities, as well as deductions for providing flexible spending accounts that can be used for dependent care.

There are tax savings for putting money into 529 plans and then using those funds for home-schooling. There is a tax credit for employers to pay people who take family leave, which was just made permanent. Many states require employers to provide paid leave for their employees. The federal government requires employers with more than 50 workers to provide unpaid leave (and hold their jobs for when employees return).

But this isn’t Vance’s priority or passion. His priority is that parents stay at home with their kids and not defer the responsibility to a child care provider. Fair enough. So instead of giving handouts for people to stay at home, wouldn’t a better approach be to expand incentives for employers?

Tax credits and deductions to pay for dependent care are fine, but I agree with Vance that there’s no better care than what a parent — at least, most parents — can provide. To that end, it would be more beneficial to explore enhanced credits for employer-funded paid parental and family leave, incentives for flexible or reduced schedules after childbirth, credits for employer-supported child care, and incentives for remote/hybrid arrangements where the job permits them.

Don’t pay parents not to work. Give employers a reason to make it easier for parents to work and raise their children at the same time.

That way people still have incentives to work and employers have the incentive to attract and retain talent. Flexibility, whether it’s working from home or expanded paid-time-off programs, is a top benefit request for most employees.

Vance isn’t wrong that young children benefit from spending more time with their parents. The question is who should pay for it and how. Instead of creating another government benefit that rewards people for leaving the workforce, we should give employers stronger incentives to provide the flexibility that lets parents remain in it.

Gene Marks is founder of the Marks Group, a small business consulting firm.

articles.title: Bret Baier presses Paxton on Trump $5K dividend payment support
articles.summary: Fox News host Bret Baier questioned Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee, on Thursday over his support for President Trump’s new controversial “Trump dividend” proposal. At the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas this week, the president floated the idea of disbursing $5,000 checks to every American adult if Republicans maintain their majority…
articles.body:
Fox News host Bret Baier questioned Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee, on Thursday over his support for President Trump’s new controversial “Trump dividend” proposal.

At the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas this week, the president floated the idea of disbursing $5,000 checks to every American adult if Republicans maintain their majority in both chambers of Congress this fall.

The idea has been met with pushback from Democrats and some conservatives, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) warning it could lead to “ more debt and more inflation ,” while left-leaning critics accuse the president of attempting to bribe the voters.

Paxton told Baier he applauded when the president introduced the idea Wednesday evening.

“I clapped because, look, the government takes too much of our money, people are hurting,” he said. “This is a way to help people with higher gas prices, higher energy costs and higher food prices.”

Baier pushed back, noting that the Texas attorney general advertises himself as a “strong fiscal conservative” who is committed to bringing down the national debt and counteracting rising inflation rates.

“Arguably, the critics of this move would say, one, it increases the deficit and debt. Two, it would really spike inflation,” the Fox News host said.

Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, has been a strong proponent of the president and his administration’s policies during his time in office and in his bid to replace incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in the primary. The Republican is up against state Rep. James Talarico (D) in a tightly contested election this November.

“I want to stop the spending, but I want to start returning more of what you earn to the taxpayer so that they can afford to live,” Paxton said. “Right now, the government is taking too high of a percentage for most of my constituents, and certainly, most of the country.”

Several GOP fiscal hawks have openly criticized the proposal, with former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) slamming it as a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

Republican Rep. Chip Roy (Texas) questioned how the U.S. government would pay for these disbursements.

“Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms,” Roy wrote Thursday on social platform X .

The president has not clarified where this money would come from. In response to a query from The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle did not provide additional details about how the proposal would work.

“President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats’ record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage,” Ingle said in a statement. “With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results.”

articles.title: Remembering the search and rescue dogs of Ground Zero
articles.summary: More than 300 dogs played vital roles in the search and recovery efforts following the September 11 terrorist attacks.
articles.body:
Editor’s note: The video above aired in a previous newscast.

NEW YORK CITY ( WPIX ) – There were many heroes on September 11, 2001, but over 300 of them were dogs, here are some of their stories.

After the chaos, nearly 100,000 workers and volunteers cleaned up Ground Zero in New York, according to the National Library of Medicine. Over 300 dogs also assisted in rescue and recovery efforts at Ground Zero, and dogs were used in recovery efforts at the Pentagon.

Dozens of search-and-rescue dogs searched the wreckage of the site for survivors.

In New York City, where most of the destruction occurred, the hours turned into days and the days into weeks.

Recovery officials realized the chance of finding survivors was increasingly slim, and the operation shifted its focus to recovery at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan.

Cadaver dogs, trained to find human remains, were also on the scene, often finding bits and pieces of victims scattered through the rubble.

“It was the most surreal thing I’ve ever seen, the most horrific act of violence I’ve ever witnessed,” said John E. Feal, whose recollection of the rescue, recovery and cleanup efforts can be found in the Library of Congress .

“The first thing I found was an entire body burned into rebar, but you had to look a couple of times. It was so unexplainable; the rubble down there. There was not a desk. There was not a chair. There was not a computer. There was not a briefcase. There was nothing but dust, concrete, rebar and papers flying around that is it,” said Christine Famiglietti, an NYPD officer who also helped during the Ground Zero cleanup effort.

Her memory of the recovery efforts is also in the Benjamin Luft collection of 9/11 oral histories, available on the Library of Congress website. She also remembers seeing long lines of volunteers passing buckets of rubble to each other to try to clear up the site.

Another participant in the oral histories said that, in the three months he spent at the recovery site, they found very few victims.

The last living person known to be rescued at Ground Zero was found by a search and rescue dog, 27 hours after both the towers collapsed, according to the 9/11 Memorial & Museum.

However, even after the last live person was found, the dogs continued working alongside their human handlers in an attempt to find life or bring peace to families searching for a lost loved one whose last known location was near or at the wreckage site.

Famiglietti, the NYPD officer, recalls that at one point the dogs, who were the unsung heroes, were getting depressed because they could not find any live survivors.

“I was down there with a guy from the 113 (precinct), and they asked for volunteers to hide in the rubble. They pulled everyone off the rubble and hid a bunch of us, and they told us to lie down like we were hurt. They then sent all the dogs in. And the dogs started barking, and life came back; everyone was clapping. Life came back to the place, and we pretended they had found us, and it was incredible; it was something that was unbelievable, moving – it really was.”

In the coming days after this American tragedy, search-and-rescue dogs, along with cadaver dogs, appeared in countless newspaper articles.

One famous photo shows a 4-year-old golden retriever, Riley, being carried out of the debris, a symbol of hope to people at the time. Riley was with FEMA’s Pennsylvania Task Force 1. Riley passed away in 2020.

Another dog, Apollo, a German shepherd with the NYPD, was the first search-and-rescue dog on the scene, along with his handler, Officer Peter Davis, according to the American Kennel Club .

“We got there right after the buildings collapsed,” Davis says. “To get to the rubble, we had to go through almost waist-deep water. All of a sudden he disappeared [and] fell into a hole. Then this big fireball came up, and he came running out. He was on fire. I brushed off the burning embers, and he went right back to searching.”

Apollo was awarded the Canine Excellence Award. He passed away at age 14, according to the AKC.

Michael Hingson, blind since birth, owned a guide dog named Roselle, who heroically led him down 78 flights of stairs to safety during 9/11. They escaped the collapsing towers and later Hingson shared their story in “Thunder Dog: The True Story of a Blind Man, His Guide Dog, and the Triumph of Trust at Ground Zero.” According to the AKC , Roselle died in 2011.

Salty, a guide dog, was with Omar Rivera on the 71st floor when a plane hit the World Trade Center. Rivera initially stayed at his desk but followed Salty when he became agitated. They ran for the stairs amid panic, and Rivera released Salty from his harness to descend alone. Salty then guided Rivera to escape just before the building collapsed. Salty passed away in 2008.

Though all the dogs that served in the 9/11 recovery effort have since passed, their tales of bravery now live on and appear in books like “ Dog Heroes of September 11 .” Multiple tales of heroic 9/11 dogs appear on many websites.

In 2011, 10 years after the attack, photographer Charlotte Dumas traveled across the U.S. to photograph the last remaining search-and-rescue dogs that had worked at the World Trade Center in her series called “ Retrieved .”

Multiple documentaries, such as “Hero Dogs of 9/11” and “9/11: True Stories of Ground Zero’s Hero Animals,” have also been produced to commemorate the amazing creatures that helped in the recovery at Ground Zero.

Sadly, Bretagne, a golden retriever and the last known living search-and-rescue dog who bravely scoured Ground Zero, was humanely euthanized on June 6, 2016, according to National Public Radio.

articles.title: Congress and our political class have been letting 9/11 families down for 25 years
articles.summary: We have watched an appearance at a ceremony matter more to many of these people than the follow-through ever has.
articles.body:
I was in my early 20s when I lost my father on Sept. 11, 2001. I have spent most of my adulthood without him or his guidance, the milestones we should have shared and the future our family expected to have together.

My father never got to meet his grandchildren. I am raising children who will never know him, but who have had to continuously absorb the horror of how he died, carrying the same sadness and injustice I have lived with for so long into another generation. His death left a hole from which we will never fully recover.

I share that not for sympathy, but because it is the lens that I cannot help but look through every year in late August and early September, when the anniversary coverage begins, and the politicians start booking their travel to New York.

This year, a few 9/11 families have publicly asked New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani not to attend today’s commemoration ceremony. I disagree. I have no issue with Mayor Mamdani being there. He was nine years old when the towers fell . Whatever one thinks of his politics today, he bears no responsibility for what happened that day, or throughout the 25 years of broken promises that have followed.

In fact, he is the only politician who has honored this anniversary appropriately, by providing long overdue truth about the air quality to survivors who have been fighting for it for so long.

I would ask that anyone reading this understand something: the families who’ve called for Mamdani to stay away speak for themselves. They do not speak for me, or for the many other 9/11 family members who see this anniversary, and this moment, very differently.

What I take issue with is the annual parade of career politicians who will be there. The people who have had real power for years and have done nothing meaningful for us with it, who will stand at that ceremony, be seen, be photographed and then vanish for the rest of the year.

These are the same people, in many cases, who welcomed Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed bin Salman into the Oval Office despite both the 9/11 families’ lawsuit against the kingdom he rules and the U.S. intelligence community’s own assessment of his role in the murder of Jamal Khashoggi. A clear slap in our faces and a signal to the world about how little accountability matters when the price is right.

The same political class has spent years blocking meaningful use and expansion of the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act , which exists specifically so families like mine can pursue accountability against foreign sponsors of terror. The same Congress has let the American Victims of Terror Compensation Act sit untouched for two years since its introduction, without a hearing, a vote or an explanation to the families waiting on it.

This is not a complete list of the failures 9/11 families have experienced from politicians who claim to care about us, it is merely the tip of the iceberg. Over two decades later, the complete list is long and devastating, and is built almost entirely of roadblocks and non-answers from people who show up every Sept. 11 to tell us they will “never forget.”

I believe them, in a narrow sense. I don’t think they have forgotten. I think they have simply decided that remembering is more useful to them as a photo opportunity, rather than a professional or ethical obligation to those they have been elected to represent.

So on this 25th anniversary, I ask that we redirect some of the scrutiny. Not away from accountability, but toward those who have long held the power to deliver 9/11 families the justice we deserve yet haven’t.

A newly elected mayor who was a child when this happened is not who failed the 9/11 community. The failure belongs to the officials and legislators who have had the ability to pass Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act reforms, move the American Victims of Terror Compensation Act , fix compensation disparities, provide us with answers and reckon honestly with a Saudi relationship so many of us still find incomprehensible, based on what our families lost. They are the elected officials who have chosen, year after year, not to do any of those things.

I don’t say this to be cynical. I say it because after spending over half of my life fighting for accountability and answers, I am tired. I’m tired of the excuses and the non-answers and the broken promises. I’m tired of believing that our politicians will one day make us the priority.

The 25-year anniversary is a heartbreaking milestone, and it feels like exactly the right moment to stop being polite about all that we have had to endure. We have watched an appearance at a ceremony matter more to many of these people than the follow-through ever has. If that’s uncomfortable for some to hear, I’d suggest the discomfort is overdue.

To those career politicians in attendance today who are reading this, know that what would truly honor my father, and the thousands who were with him in the towers isn’t your presence at a ceremony. It’s what you do with the other 364 days of the year.

Kathleen Coppo Zapata lost her father Joseph Coppo in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

articles.title: Former DHS chiefs: New public safety agency needed
articles.summary: Former heads of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) called for a public safety agency to be established on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. In a joint interview with NBC News on Thursday, former DHS Secretaries Michael Chertoff and Jeh Johnson discussed the current direction of the agency, which they…
articles.body:
Former heads of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) called for a public safety agency to be established on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks .

In a joint interview with NBC News on Thursday, former DHS Secretaries Michael Chertoff and Jeh Johnson discussed the current direction of the agency, which they both said “has gotten off track.”

Johnson, who served under former President Obama from 2013 to 2017, said he believes the agency needs “a reset.”

“When I stepped into the job of secretary in 2013, the department was still, I think, viewed primarily as security,” he said. “Now I fear in many communities DHS has become a pariah, radioactive, the department of mass deportations, heartless, locking up kids, and that is one of the reasons why I think we need a reset.”

The Deportation Data Project found that Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which falls under the DHS, had arrested 49,571 people in July, the highest such number during President Trump’s second term.

Chertoff and Johnson asked for any agency that did not fall under the realm of public safety to be spun off, including the Federal Emergency Management Agency, resembling a European model of public safety ministries.

Chertoff, who served under former President George W. Bush from 2005 to 2009, said he believed it “would help the Cabinet secretary deconflict, unify and achieve a common effort of priorities in terms of where to protect the country and how to reduce the most serious threats that we would be facing.”

“We’re spending most of our time worrying about gardeners and home health aides and getting them thrown out of the country, as opposed to focusing on people that actually are doing a lot of damage,” he added.

Their comments come as America mourns the loss of 2,977 lives in the attacks on the World Trade Center in New York City; the Pentagon in Arlington, Va.; and at the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93 in Pennsylvania.

When asked if the modern DHS could handle another attack of this magnitude, Johnson said he believes it could because “we are better at tracking who enters the country.”

“The problem, however, is the terrorist threat morphed, and the DHS that Secretary Chertoff and I led years ago is not equipped to deal with that form of domestic terrorism,” he said.

DHS did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

articles.title: Nashville airport board unanimously approves Dolly Parton name change
articles.summary: Nashville’s airport board voted Friday to unanimously approve the renaming of the city’s airport after the late country star Dolly Parton. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) proposed the name change shortly after Parton died last month at the age of 80 following a brief battle with cancer. The Metro Nashville Airport Authority’s vote marks the…
articles.body:
Nashville’s airport board voted Friday to unanimously approve the renaming of the city’s airport after the late country star Dolly Parton.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) proposed the name change shortly after Parton died last month at the age of 80 following a brief battle with cancer.

The Metro Nashville Airport Authority’s vote marks the first formal step toward dedicating Nashville International Airport to the iconic artist, who was born and raised in the Volunteer State.

The new name will be jointly determined by airport leaders and the Dollywood Foundation, a nonprofit organization started by the late country artist in 1988.

In a statement last month announcing the renaming proposal, Lee said Parton’s “extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state.”

Parton was raised in a one-room cabin in Sevier County, Tenn., alongside her 11 siblings. She lived in Nashville up until her death and has made significant contributions to the state through her nonprofit organization’s Imagination Library and college scholarships.

“From her rural mountain home in East Tennessee to global stages, Dolly carried the Volunteer Spirit with her,” the governor wrote.

“At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness,” he continued.

Before Parton’s death, there was a public push to dedicate the airport to the iconic country music artist. A petition supporting this renaming effort garnered more than 175,000 signatures.

Parton’s sister, Stella Parton, told CBS News’s Gayle King this week she thinks the renaming is a “great idea.”

“I think we ought to name it ‘United States of Dolly Parton,’ since you know, somebody else is naming everything something else,” she said, in an apparent criticism of President Trump’s recent push to rename Lake Ontario and New Mexico .

“The state of Dolly Parton,” she continued. “Let’s change the name of the state.”

articles.title: Epstein survivors back Talarico, urge Paxton to sue DOJ over redacted files
articles.summary: Democratic State Representative James Talarico and Jeffrey Epstein survivors used a traveling exhibit in Dallas to call on Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to support them and sue the Department of Justice over the handling of Epstein’s files.
articles.body:
DALLAS (Nexstar) — Victims and survivors who say they were abused by Jeffrey Epstein are supporting Democratic State Rep. James Talarico in his bid for Texas Senate over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico and the survivors also called on Paxton to use his current office to sue the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) over their Epstein file redactions.

In May, the Donald J. Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room opened in New York City, featuring the entire printed version of the released Epstein files. On Thursday, the 3,437 books lined an event space in Dallas, the first stop on the exhibit’s swing state tour.

The timing appeared intentional. The day before, President Donald Trump spoke for nearly two hours just a few miles away at his GOP midterm convention. The exhibit features a timeline showing the relationship between Trump and Epstein over the decades.

“When did pedophilia become a partisan issue?” Talarico said to reporters at the exhibit. “When did holding sexual abusers accountable become controversial? When did Ken Paxton decide it was okay to ignore these survivors?”

In response to Talarico and the Epstein survivors, the Paxton campaign questioned the authenticity of Talarico’s concerns.

“If James Talarico was really concerned about the survivors of Epstein’s horrific crimes, his campaign infrastructure wouldn’t have taken over $11.5 million from Epstein’s long time associate, Reid Hoffman. Now, James Talarico continues to lie to Texans about his radical record with the help of Epstein money. It’s disgusting that the man claiming to run a campaign against billionaires is bought and paid for by Epstein’s billionaire buddy,” Campaign spokesperson Madison Cercy said.

While Hoffman has donated a significant amount to Lone Star Rising PAC, a Talarico-aligned Super PAC, he has not donated to Talarico’s campaign directly. By law, Talarico cannot coordinate with the PAC, including who the PAC decides to accept money from.

Talarico’s campaign also noted that the candidate has pledged to help ban super PACs should he defeat Paxton.

Survivor Sharlene Rochard also accused Paxton of not accepting an invitation to meet with the survivors.

Rochard’s criticism came after another survivor, Annie Farmer, said Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, also declined to meet with the group this summer regarding concerns about Trump’s attorney general pick, Todd Blanche. According to Politico , Blanche met with Epstein associate and convicted sex offender Ghislaine Maxwell right before her move to a minimum-security federal prison camp in Texas.

“Texans need leaders that will send a strong message to survivors of these crimes that no matter how powerful the perpetrator, accountability will be pursued,” Farmer said.

In his brief remarks, Talarico made two direct asks of Paxton.

“Today, I am calling on Ken Paxton to stop ignoring these survivors and their requests to meet,” he said. “And I’m calling on him to use his power as attorney general to sue the Department of Justice over the mishandling of these Epstein files.”

The survivors and Talarico raised concerns on two fronts. Talarico expressed concerns over 2.5 million files that have not been released, while survivors also criticized the Department of Justice for failing to redact some victims’ personal information.

Dani Bensky says she experienced this firsthand. The former ballerina met Epstein at 17 years old and says she was pressured to recruit new girls in exchange for preferential medical treatment for her mother.

“Every single time that it was an awful heinous crime, the email address is redacted and you can’t see who it’s coming from,” she said. “But all of my identifying information was out there, like my name, my phone number, where I went to school, where I was working.”

She said nude photos of young girls were also released by the DOJ.

“(The exhibit’s director) was walking BBC through the files and he opened a page just to show it’s not a prop book… opened up a page and it was like 800 photos of young nude girls. So who is our government protecting?”

articles.title: Mamdani and Giuliani shake hands at 9/11 commemoration
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Mayor Rudy Giuliani shook hands during the 9/11 commemoration ceremony at Ground Zero, a show of unity after Giuliani called on Mamdani not to attend the memorial. Giuliani, who was mayor during the Sept. 11 attack, told Newsmax earlier this week, “having lost friends there, and being…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Mayor Rudy Giuliani shook hands during the 9/11 commemoration ceremony at Ground Zero, a show of unity after Giuliani called on Mamdani not to attend the memorial.

Giuliani, who was mayor during the Sept. 11 attack, told Newsmax earlier this week, “having lost friends there, and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”

“Frankly, whatever he’d like to say, he doesn’t agree that Sept. 11 was an Islamic terrorist attack on the United States of America,” Giuliani said in the interview with Newsmax on Sunday.

Giuliani’s criticism was heavily tinged with anti-Muslim sentiment and false claims about Mamdani’s beliefs.

“They have every desire to take us over. This is not, they want to be just another religion, they want to dominate us,” Giuliani said of Muslims. “Mamdani is a clear supporter of that.”

The calls from Giuliani and others urging Mamdani to skip the ceremony stem in part from the mayor’s appointment of Ramzi Kassem, who previously represented a convicted al-Qaeda member whose brother-in-law was among the 19 hijackers who perpetrated the Sept. 11 attack, as the city’s top legal counsel.

The move led some families of 9/11 victims to launch a petition urging Mamdani not to go. The petition claims Mamdani supports people perceived as “dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies.”

Giuliani, who led New York City when the attacks took place, has touted conspiracy theories tinged with anti-Muslim sentiment about Mamdani in connection with the attacks and said it offended him that the mayor will attend.

In the week leading up to the memorial, some families of 9/11 victims to launch a petition urging Mamdani not to go. The petition claims Mamdani supports people perceived as “dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies.”

The calls from Giuliani urging Mamdani to skip the ceremony stem in part from the mayor’s appointment of Ramzi Kassem , who previously represented a convicted al-Qaeda member whose brother-in-law was among the 19 hijackers who perpetrated the Sept. 11 attack, as the city’s top legal counsel.

Mamdani has dismissed the calls for him not to attend, saying the focus leading up to Friday’s commemoration should be on the victims of the attack and their families, as well as first responders. He then told reporters he “did not have much more to add” when asked about Giuliani’s comments.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) and others have defended Mamdani from these attacks and said he should be in attendance.

“Division should not prevail over the spirit of unity that brought us together after September 11th,” Hochul said in a post on the social platform X. “On this 25th anniversary, we should honor those we lost by coming together again as New Yorkers and Americans. The Mayor of New York City will be there, as he should be.”

On Tuesday, Mamdani’s office also released records , with the mayor’s fiscal 2027 budget, that show city leaders “lied” about the air quality in Manhattan in the weeks after the attack on the World Trade Center.

“It would be one thing if government had stood alongside survivors and provided them with everything they needed at every step of the way,” Mamdani added, noting that “could not be further” from what occurred.

The released documents include records from Giuliani’s administration who led NYC during the time of the attacks.

When a reporter asked Mamdani about whether Giuliani lied about air quality after Sept. 11, the incumbent mayor said, “I leave it to New Yorkers to make their judgements.”
